name: French (Switzerland)
family: Indo-European, Romance, Western Romance, Gallo-Romance (langue d'oïl)
variety: French of western Switzerland (Suisse romande), centred on the cantons of Vaud and Neuchâtel where most of the described features are found; Geneva is closer to the French of France
sources: Fougeron, Cécile and Smith, Caroline L. (1993). French. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 23(2), 73-76. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association (1999), Cambridge University Press.
Métral, Jean-Pierre (1977). Le vocalisme du français en Suisse romande: considérations phonologiques. Cahiers Ferdinand de Saussure 31.

Andreassen, Helene N.; Maître, Raphaël; Racine, Isabelle (2010). La Suisse. In Detey, Durand, Laks and Lyche (eds.), Les variétés du français parlé dans l'espace francophone: ressources pour l'enseignement. Paris: Ophrys.

Racine, Isabelle and Andreassen, Helene N. (2012). A phonological study of a Swiss French variety: data from the canton of Neuchâtel. In Gess, Lyche and Meisenburg (eds.), Phonological Variation in French: Illustrations from Three Continents. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Schwab, Sandra and Racine, Isabelle (2013). Le débit lent des Suisses romands: mythe ou réalité? Journal of French Language Studies 23(2).
Walter, Henriette (1982). Enquête phonologique et variétés régionales du français. Paris: Presses Universitaires de France.
Simon, Anne Catherine (ed.) (2012). La variation prosodique régionale en français. Bruxelles: De Boeck-Duculot.
Jun, Sun-Ah and Fougeron, Cécile (2002). Realizations of accentual phrase in French intonation. Probus 14, 147-172.
Delais-Roussarie, Elisabeth et al. (2015). Intonational phonology of French: developing a ToBI system for French. In Frota and Prieto (eds.), Intonation in Romance. Oxford University Press.
Calliope (1989). La parole et son traitement automatique. Paris: Masson.
Grabe, Esther and Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the rhythm class hypothesis. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male, reference French of France (means over speakers)
vowel_formants.source: Calliope 1989; no table for Swiss speakers is cited, so these are stand-in values for the oral vowels that Swiss and reference French share (no value for the back /ɑ/)

contrasts: four nasal vowels: /ɛ̃/ and /œ̃/ are kept apart (brin versus brun)
front /a/ versus back /ɑ/, the second also long (patte [pat] versus pâte [pɑːt], tache versus tâche)
/ɛ/ versus long /ɛː/ (mettre versus maître, faite versus fête)
/e/ versus /ɛ/ in final open syllables (piqué versus piquais, né versus naît)
/o/ versus /ɔ/ at the end of a word, which reference French lacks: peau [po] versus pot [pɔ], maux versus mot, saut versus sot (Vaud, Neuchâtel, Fribourg, Valais)
vowel length at the end of a word: a final vowel followed by written e is long or ends in a glide (ami [ami] versus amie [amiː] or [amij], nu versus nue, bout versus boue, armé versus armée)
/o/ versus /ɔ/ and /ø/ versus /œ/ in closed syllables (côte versus cote, jeûne versus jeune)
allophony: long final vowels of feminine forms are often realised with a closing glide, above all in Vaud: amie [amij], journée [ʒuʁnej]
vowels are long before final /ʁ z ʒ v/ as in reference French
/ʁ/ is a uvular fricative, voiceless next to voiceless consonants
/ɥ/ is kept before /i/ (huit, lui) by most speakers
the long final vowels go back to a lost final schwa, written e (amie, nue, armée)
phonotactics: schwa can be dropped when the resulting cluster is allowed, as in reference French
liaison and enchaînement link a final consonant to a following vowel
word-final obstruent plus liquid clusters (quatre, table) are simplified in everyday speech

stress.rule: The last full syllable of each accentual phrase is prominent; many Swiss speakers add a prominence (higher pitch, extra length) on the penultimate syllable of the phrase.
stress.cues: lengthening of the final syllable and a pitch movement on it; pitch and length on the penultimate syllable in the regional pattern

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in quality; schwa can be dropped
rhythm.notes: Schwab and Racine (2013) test the common belief that Swiss speakers talk slowly and find a slower articulation rate for their Swiss speakers than for Parisians. The nPVI figure is for a speaker from France and is given for orientation only.

npvi_v.source: Grabe and Low 2002 (one speaker of French from France, not Swiss French)

length.notes: Length is contrastive for final vowels (amie, nue, boue, armée) and for /ɛ/ versus /ɛː/; /ɑ/ is long as well as back. No duration ratio is cited here.

intonation.declarative: a rise on the last syllable of each non-final accentual phrase and a fall to low on the last syllable of the utterance; in the regional pattern the penultimate syllable of a phrase is high or long before the final movement
intonation.yes_no_question: with statement word order, a rise on the last syllable to a high boundary; with est-ce que or inversion the rise is smaller or the contour falls
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then a fall to a low ending; a final rise is also possible
intonation.continuation: rise on the last syllable of the phrase, larger at major boundaries
intonation.accent_shape: LH* on the last full syllable of the accentual phrase, with an optional initial rise LHi; regional prominence on the penultimate syllable
intonation.notes: The phonological system is that of French in general (Jun and Fougeron 2002; Delais-Roussarie et al. 2015). Regional studies are collected in Simon (2012).

problems: the voice is the voice of France with other number words: the only conditional entries for Switzerland are septante, huitante and nonante in the word list; phonemes, rules and tunes are shared
brin and brun get different phoneme names (E~ and W~, printed [ɛ̃] and [œ̃]), but both phonemes play the same vowel data (vnasal/W_n) with the same length, so the contrast cannot be heard
there is no back /ɑ/: pâte differs from patte only by a length mark on the same front [a] ([pˈaːt] against [pˈat])
no long /ɛː/: mettre and maître, faite and fête are identical
no final /ɔ/: peau and pot, maux and mot, saut and sot are all [o]
no length or glide in final vowels: ami and amie, nu and nue, bout and boue, armé and armée are identical
rose and chose have open [ɔ] ([ʁˈɔz], [ʃˈɔz]) where Swiss French has long close [oː]
jeune is given the close vowel [ø], so jeune and jeûne differ only by length; the contrast is [œ] versus [øː]
the slower rate and the penultimate prominence reported for Swiss speakers are not modelled
80 is always huitante, which is the usage of Vaud, Valais and Fribourg; Geneva, Neuchâtel and the Jura say quatre-vingts
good: 70 and 90 are read septante and nonante
/e/ and /ɛ/ are kept apart in final syllables (piqué against piquais, né against naît)
côte [koːt] and cote [kɔt] differ; /ɥ/ is kept before i
prominence is phrase-final and the French tune set is used

notes: Swiss French keeps more vowel contrasts than any other major variety of French: four nasal vowels, two a vowels, length, and open versus close o at the end of words. None of them except the a contrast (by length only) is present in the eSpeak NG voice.
